content: Tannins are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds that are astringent and bitter in taste. They have the ability to bind and precipitate proteins. The term tannin originates from their historical use in the tanning of animal hides to produce leather. Chemically, tannins are large polyphenolic molecules with sufficient hydroxyl and carboxyl groups to form strong complexes with proteins and other macromolecules. Their molecular weights range from 500 to over 3,000. Tannins are broadly categorized into two types: hydrolyzable tannins and condensed tannins (also known as proanthocyanidins). Hydrolyzable Tannins Hydrolyzable tannins are characterized by a central polyol carbohydrate core, typically D-glucose. The hydroxyl groups of this carbohydrate are partially or fully esterified with phenolic acids such as gallic acid (in gallotannins) or ellagic acid (in ellagitannins). These tannins can be hydrolyzed by weak acids or bases, yielding carbohydrates and phenolic acids. An example of a hydrolyzable tannin is tannic acid, which consists of gallic acid esters of glucose and is found in the leaves and bark of various plant species. Condensed Tannins Condensed tannins, or proanthocyanidins, are polymers composed of 2 to 50 or more flavonoid units linked by carbon-carbon bonds. These bonds are resistant to hydrolysis. While most condensed tannins are water-soluble, some larger polymers are insoluble. Unlike hydrolyzable tannins, condensed tannins are not easily broken down. Tannins in Foods Tea The tea plant (Camellia sinensis) is naturally rich in tannins. When tea leaves are steeped in hot water, the resulting brew has a characteristic astringent or tart flavor due to the presence of catechins and other flavonoids. However, the tannins in tea are chemically distinct from tannic acid, and tea extracts have been shown to contain no tannic acid. Wine Tannins, particularly condensed tannins, are abundant in wine, especially red wine. These tannins originate from grape skins and seeds, with the latter contributing harsher tannins. Red wines, which are fermented with grape skins and seeds, tend to have more noticeable tannins. Condensed tannins in wine are polymers of procyanidin monomers, while hydrolyzable tannins are extracted from oak barrels used for aging. Hydrolyzable tannins are more prone to oxidation than condensed tannins. Modern winemaking techniques aim to minimize undesirable tannins from grape seeds by gently crushing the grapes. Wines aged in oak barrels may also acquire tannins from the wood. Tannins play a crucial role in preventing oxidation during wine aging and contribute to the sediment found in aged wines. Research has shown that procyanidins, a type of tannin, have vascular health benefits by suppressing the production of peptides responsible for arterial hardening. Wines from regions like southwest France and Sardinia, which are rich in procyanidins, are associated with longer life spans in their populations. Fruits Pomegranates Pomegranates are rich in hydrolyzable tannins, with punicalagins being the most abundant. Punicalagins, which have a molecular weight of 1038, are the largest molecules found intact in rat plasma after oral ingestion. Studies have shown that punicalagins are non-toxic, even when included in a 6% diet for 37 days in rats. These compounds are the primary contributors to the antioxidant and health benefits of pomegranate juice. Dietary supplements and nutritional products often contain pomegranate extracts standardized to punicalagins, which are recognized as safe (GRAS) by the U.S. FDA. It is recommended to use pomegranate extracts that mimic the natural polyphenol ratio of the fruit, as synergistic effects have been observed in such formulations. Persimmons Certain persimmon varieties, such as Korean, American, and Hachiya (Japanese), are highly astringent and inedible unless fully ripe. This astringency is due to their high tannin content. Consuming unripe persimmons can cause a dry mouth sensation, as the tannins bind to salivary proteins, rendering them ineffective. Berries Berries, including cranberries, strawberries, and blueberries, contain both hydrolyzable and condensed tannins. Nutritional Implications Excessive consumption of tannins can inhibit the absorption of minerals, such as iron, due to their ability to chelate metal ions. Tannin-chelated metal ions are not bioavailable. However, this property may be beneficial during infections, as the immune system sequesters iron to limit microbial growth. Tannins also precipitate proteins, which can reduce nutrient absorption in ruminant animals consuming high-tannin grains like sorghum. Industrial and Medicinal Uses Tannins are essential in leather tanning, with oak bark being a traditional source. They are also used medicinally in antidiarrheal, hemostatic, and antihemorrhoidal formulations. Tannins react with ferric chloride to produce various colors, depending on the type of tannin. Iron gall ink, for example, is made by treating tannin solutions with iron(II) sulfate. Additionally, tannins are used in industrial adhesives, such as those developed for particleboard. Potential Medical Applications Tannins, including galloand ellagic acid derivatives, have shown inhibitory effects on HIV replication. Compounds such as 1,3,4-tri-O-galloylquinic acid, 3,5-di-O-galloyl-shikimic acid, 3,4,5-tri-O-galloylshikimic acid, punicalin, and punicalagin have been found to inhibit HIV replication in infected H9 lymphocytes with minimal cytotoxicity. Punicalin and punicacortein C have also demonstrated the ability to inhibit purified HIV reverse transcriptase.
